source.title: Deep Neural Networks with Multi-Branch Architectures Are Less Non-Convex
source.authors: Hongyang Zhang; Jun-Ru Shao; R. Salakhutdinov

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies the width of one-hidden-layer ReLU networks and reports how often SGD reaches a known global minimum, a different measure of width-related optimization outcomes than the claim version specifies.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports loss-landscape visualizations and CIFAR-10 test accuracy, but neither gives a training-classification-error result. CIFAR-10 test accuracy is not a row for these versions.
record.test_reason: Section 5.2 tests V2's width-related optimization question using SGD global-optimum hitting rates for ReLU students learning data from an 11-neuron teacher. This differs from certifying convergence to spurious local minima. Students with 12 and 13 neurons directly test the one- and two-extra-neuron conditions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's empirical paraphrase is accurate but omits the main theoretical conclusions: under specified assumptions, the normalized duality gap decreases with branch count for multi-branch networks with τ-hinge loss, and strong duality holds for the studied regularized deep linear networks. The synthetic SGD experiment reports greater global-optimum hitting frequency with width.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SGD on a synthetic one-hidden-layer ReLU teacher-generated dataset and measures global-minimum hitting frequency, rather than directly measuring spurious-local-minimum outcomes as in the claim version.
record.method_sensitivity: Hidden-neuron count changes global-minimum hitting frequency.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 1 bounds the normalized duality gap by 2/I under its assumptions; Figures 1 and 4 show increasingly convex-looking two-dimensional loss projections.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing branch count reduces a duality-gap bound and apparent non-convexity in selected loss projections; these measures do not establish SGD's spurious-minimum frequency.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 2 establishes strong duality for specified regularized deep linear networks, with numerical agreement between primal and dual solutions in Appendix A.2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Specified regularized deep linear optimization problems admit exact convex dual formulations.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A.1 reports increasing CIFAR-10 test accuracy with more parallel VGG-9 branches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing parallel branch count improves test accuracy in the tested VGG-9 architectures.

record.problems: The width sweep uses a synthetic dataset with one 11-hidden-neuron teacher and 100 initialization seeds per width; the reported metric is global-minimum hitting, not spurious-minimum frequency. The empirical loss-landscape evidence is visualized rather than numerically quantified.

untested.parts: Training classification error of convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including random or corrupted labels and training-recipe effects.
Increasing teacher and student widths together; certified spurious-local-minimum frequencies; the original gradient-descent and initialization protocol. Only one teacher width is tested.
Depth-related training degradation and comparisons involving identity shortcuts, special tanh initialization, or Fixup.
Comparisons of initialization schemes, signal or gradient propagation, training speed, and trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, catapult dynamics, sharpness trajectories, and divergence.
Batch normalization versus matched unnormalized networks for training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source. Table 1's values are correctly extracted. The record incorrectly treats the one- and two-extra-neuron conditions as untested. No reported failure rate should be equated with a certified spurious-local-minimum rate. The supplied text contains CIFAR-10 test-accuracy results, not training-classification-error results.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, and effects of model size or training duration on that error.

The tested network widths are 10–21 hidden neurons, not the stated 6–20 range; the paper reports global-minimum hitting frequency rather than frequency of ending in spurious local minima, and does not test the stated one- or two-neuron student-over-teacher margin directly.
Depth and identity shortcuts, plain versus residual networks, and normalization choices.
Initialization schemes and their effects on training speed or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability limits, loss rises, curvature, sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

relationships.condition: An 11-neuron teacher with students of width 12 or 13; SGD for 100,000 iterations.
relationships.reason: R2–R4 show success rising from 9/100 to 21/100 and 24/100: one or two extra neurons help incompletely, with 79% and 76% still missing the optimum; failures are not certified local minima.
relationships.display_finding: Global-optimum success rose from 9/100 to 21/100 and 24/100 with one and two extra neurons, leaving failure rates of 79% and 76% without certifying local minima.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: An 11-neuron teacher with students of width 12 or 13; SGD for 100,000 iterations.
source_check.reason: R2–R4 show success increasing from 9/100 to 21/100 and 24/100. The small width increases help incompletely; unsuccessful runs are not certified spurious minima.

relationships.condition: Larger width increases: an 11-neuron teacher with students of width 19–21.
relationships.reason: R2 and R10–R12 support the width-benefit component: global-optimum success increases from 9/100 at equal width to 52/100, 64/100, and 75/100.
relationships.display_finding: Global-optimum success rose from 9/100 at equal width to 52/100, 64/100, and 75/100 at student widths 19, 20, and 21, respectively.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Larger width increases: an 11-neuron teacher with students of width 19–21.
source_check.reason: R2 and R10–R12 show substantially higher global-minimum success with wider students: 9/100 versus 52/100, 64/100 and 75/100. This supports the general width benefit; width 21 extends beyond V2's stated range.

relationships.condition: Students of width 14–18 learning from the fixed 11-neuron teacher.
relationships.reason: R2 and R5–R9 show only 24–35/100 successes versus 9/100 at equal width, so substantial optimization failure persists despite three to seven extra neurons.
relationships.display_finding: With three to seven extra student neurons, global-optimum success remained at 24–35/100 versus 9/100 at equal width.

tranche.reason: Section 5.2 tests the width-related optimization question using fixed-teacher SGD global-minimum hitting frequencies, differing from the original gradient-descent and local-minimum endpoint protocol.

source_check.notes: Success means reaching the known global minimum within 1 × 10⁻⁵ after 100,000 SGD iterations under the synthetic hinge-loss setup. The fixed-teacher sweep neither tests joint teacher/student growth nor certifies failed runs as local minima; statement checks cover only this study's contribution.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic teacher network with 11 hidden neurons; student widths 10–21
reader_labels.reason: The fraction of SGD runs hitting the known global minimum generally rises with width, from 2 / 100 at 10 neurons to 75 / 100 at 21 neurons (R1–R12). The reported metric is global-minimum hitting, so this supports the width-related optimization trend but does not directly measure spurious-minimum frequency.
